blocks.p: Now, as Christian was walking on alone, he saw someone far off coming across the field to meet him, and it happened that they met just where their paths crossed. The gentleman who met him was named Mr. Worldly Wiseman. He lived in the town of Expediency, a very large town, and close to the place Christian had come from. This man had some idea who Christian was, for Christian’s leaving the City of Destruction had been much talked about, not only in the town where he lived but in other places too. So Mr. Worldly Wiseman, guessing who he was from his labored walk, his sighs and groans, and the like, began to talk with him.
“Well now, my good fellow, where are you going, weighed down like that?”

“Weighed down indeed, as much as any poor creature ever was, I think! And since you ask where I’m going, I’ll tell you, sir: I’m going to that Wicket Gate ahead of me; for there, I’m told, I’ll be shown a way to be rid of my heavy burden.”
“Do you have a wife and children?”
“Yes; but this burden weighs on me so heavily that I can’t take the pleasure in them I used to. It’s as if I had none.” [1 Cor. 7:29]
“Will you listen to me if I give you some advice?”
“If it’s good, I will; for I need good advice.”
“Then I would advise you to get rid of your burden as quickly as you can. You’ll never have peace of mind until you do, and you’ll never be able to enjoy the blessings God has given you until then.”

“That’s exactly what I’m looking for, to be rid of this heavy burden. But I can’t get it off myself, and there’s no one in our country who can take it off my shoulders. That’s why I’m going this way, as I told you, so that I can be rid of it.”
“Who told you to go this way to be rid of your burden?”
“A man who seemed to me a very great and honorable person. His name, as I remember, is Evangelist.”

“Curse him for his advice! There is no more dangerous and troublesome road in the world than the one he has sent you on, and you’ll find that out if you follow his counsel. You’ve run into something already, I see, for the mud of the Swamp of Despair is all over you; and that swamp is only the beginning of the sorrows that come to those who go that way. Listen to me; I’m older than you. On the road you’re taking, you’re likely to meet with weariness, pain, hunger, danger, nakedness, the sword, lions, dragons, darkness, and in a word, death, and who knows what else! These things are certainly true; many witnesses have confirmed them. And why should a man throw his life away so carelessly by listening to a stranger?”
“Why, sir, this burden on my back is more terrible to me than all the things you’ve mentioned. I don’t care what I meet on the way, so long as I also meet with deliverance from my burden.”
“How did you come by this burden in the first place?”
“By reading this book in my hand.”

“I thought so. It has happened to you as it happens to other weak men, who meddle with things too high for them and suddenly fall into the same distractions you have. And those distractions not only unman them, as I see yours have done to you, but drive them into desperate ventures to get they know not what.”
“I know what I want to get. It is relief from my heavy burden.”

“But why look for relief this way, when so many dangers come with it? Especially since, if you’d only have the patience to hear me out, I could direct you to what you want without the dangers you’ll run into on this road. Yes, and the remedy is close at hand. What’s more, instead of those dangers, you’ll find plenty of safety, friendship, and contentment.”
“Please, sir, tell me this secret.”

“Well, in that village over there, the village called Morality, there lives a gentleman named Legality, a very sensible man with a very good reputation, who has the skill to help men get burdens like yours off their shoulders. To my knowledge he has done a great deal of good that way. Yes, and besides that, he has the skill to cure those whose burdens have turned their wits a little. You can go to him, as I said, and be helped right away. His house is less than a mile from here. And if he isn’t home himself, he has a fine young son named Civility, who can do it, so to speak, as well as the old gentleman himself. There, I tell you, you can be eased of your burden. And if you don’t want to go back to your old home, as indeed I wouldn’t advise you to, you can send for your wife and children to join you in that village. There are houses standing empty there now, and you can have one at a reasonable price. Food is cheap and good there too; and what will make your life happier still is that you’ll be sure to live among honest neighbors, respected and in good standing.”
Christian was somewhat at a loss now; but he soon concluded, “If what this gentleman says is true, my wisest course is to take his advice.” And so he spoke again.
“Sir, which way is it to this honest man’s house?”
“Do you see that hill over there?”
“Yes, very clearly.”
“You go by that hill, and the first house you come to is his.”

So Christian turned out of his way to go to Mr. Legality’s house for help. But when he had come close to the hill, it seemed so high, and the side of it next to the road hung over so far, that Christian was afraid to go any further in case the hill fell on his head. So he stood still there and did not know what to do. His burden also seemed heavier now than it had while he was on the right road. And flashes of fire came out of the hill, which made Christian afraid he would be burned. [Ex. 19:16, 18] There he stood, sweating and shaking with fear. [Heb. 12:21]

v: When Christians listen to the worldly-wise,
they leave their road, and pay for it in sighs;
for Master Worldly Wiseman’s way can show
a saint the road to bondage and to woe.

blocks.p: And now he began to regret that he had taken Mr. Worldly Wiseman’s advice. Just then he saw Evangelist coming to meet him, and at the sight of him he blushed with shame. Evangelist came nearer and nearer, and when he reached him he looked at him with a stern and terrible face, and began to reason with him.
“What are you doing here, Christian?” he said.
Christian did not know what to answer, and stood speechless before him.
Then Evangelist went on: “Aren’t you the man I found crying outside the walls of the City of Destruction?”
“Yes, dear sir, I am the man.”
“Didn’t I show you the way to the little Wicket Gate?”
“Yes, dear sir,” said Christian.
“Then how is it that you have turned aside so quickly? For you are off the road now.”
“I met a gentleman as soon as I had got over the Swamp of Despair, who persuaded me that in the village ahead I might find a man who could take off my burden.”
“What was he?”

“He looked like a gentleman, and he talked to me a great deal, and at last he got me to give in. So I came here. But when I saw this hill, and how it hangs over the road, I stopped short in case it fell on my head.”
“What did that gentleman say to you?”
“Why, he asked me where I was going, and I told him.”
“And what did he say then?”
“He asked me if I had a family, and I told him. ‘But,’ I said, ‘I’m so weighed down with the burden on my back that I can’t take pleasure in them as I used to.’”
“And what did he say then?”

“He told me to get rid of my burden quickly, and I told him that relief was what I was looking for. ‘That’s why I’m going to that gate,’ I said, ‘to get further directions about how to reach the place of deliverance.’ Then he said he would show me a better way, and a shorter one, without as many difficulties as the way, sir, that you set me on. ‘This way,’ he said, ‘will take you to the house of a gentleman who has the skill to take off these burdens.’ So I believed him, and turned out of that road into this one, hoping I might be eased of my burden soon. But when I came to this place and saw things as they really are, I stopped, as I said, for fear of danger. And now I don’t know what to do.”
“Then stand still a moment,” said Evangelist, “so that I can show you the words of God.”
So Christian stood there trembling.

“’See that you do not refuse the One who speaks,’” said Evangelist. “’For if they did not escape when they refused the one who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we turn away from the One who warns us from heaven.’ [Heb. 12:25] And again: ‘My righteous one will live by faith; but if he shrinks back, my soul will take no pleasure in him.’” [Heb. 10:38]

Then he applied these words to him. “You are the man who is running into this misery. You have begun to reject the counsel of the Most High, and to draw your foot back from the way of peace, to the point of almost risking your eternal ruin.”
Then Christian fell down at his feet as if dead, crying, “Woe is me, for I am ruined!”
At this Evangelist caught him by the right hand and said, “’Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven.’ [Matt. 12:31; Mark 3:28] ‘Stop doubting, and believe.’” [John 20:27]
Then Christian revived a little, and stood up trembling before Evangelist, as before.

“Pay closer attention to what I am going to tell you,” Evangelist went on. “I will show you now who it was that deceived you, and who it was he sent you to. The man who met you is called Worldly Wiseman, and the name suits him: partly because he has a taste only for the teaching of this world [1 John 4:5], which is why he always goes to church in the town of Morality; and partly because he loves that teaching best, since it best saves him from the cross. [Gal. 6:12] And because he has this worldly temper, he tries to twist my ways, though they are right. Now there are three things in this man’s advice that you must utterly reject:
1. His turning you off the road.
2. His working to make the cross hateful to you.
3. His setting your feet on the road that leads to the ministry of death.

“First, you must reject his turning you off the road, and your own consent to it, because that means rejecting the counsel of God for the counsel of a Worldly Wiseman. The Lord says, ‘Strive to enter through the narrow gate’ [Luke 13:24], the gate I sent you to; ‘for narrow is the gate that leads to life, and only a few find it.’ [Matt. 7:14] This wicked man turned you away from that little Wicket Gate, and from the road leading to it, and almost brought you to destruction. So hate his turning you off the road, and hate yourself for listening to him.

“Second, you must reject his working to make the cross hateful to you; for you are to value it more highly than ‘the treasures of Egypt.’ [Heb. 11:25-26] Besides, the King of glory has told you that whoever ‘wants to save his life will lose it’ [Mark 8:35; John 12:25; Matt. 10:39]; and, ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters, yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.’ [Luke 14:26] So when a man works to persuade you that the very thing will be your death without which, as the Truth himself has said, you cannot have eternal life, you must reject that teaching.

“Third, you must hate his setting your feet on the road that leads to the ministry of death. And for this you must consider whom he sent you to, and how unable that person is to deliver you from your burden.

“The one he sent you to for relief, Legality by name, is the son of the slave woman, who is in slavery to this day along with her children [Gal. 4:21-27]; and, figuratively, she is this very Mount Sinai you were afraid would fall on your head. Now if she and her children are slaves, how can you expect them to set you free? This Legality, then, cannot free you from your burden. No one has ever been rid of his burden by him, and no one ever will be. You cannot be made right with God by keeping the law; by the works of the law no living person can be rid of his burden. So Mr. Worldly Wiseman is a stranger to the truth, and Mr. Legality is a fraud; and as for his son Civility, for all his simpering looks, he is only a hypocrite and cannot help you. Believe me, there is nothing in all the talk you have heard from these foolish men except a scheme to cheat you of your salvation by turning you off the road I set you on.”

After this, Evangelist called aloud to heaven to confirm what he had said; and at that, words and fire came out of the mountain under which poor Christian stood, so that the hair on his skin stood up. These were the words: “All who rely on the works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.’” [Gal. 3:10]

Now Christian expected nothing but death, and began to cry out bitterly, even cursing the hour he had met Mr. Worldly Wiseman, and calling himself a thousand times a fool for listening to his advice. He was also deeply ashamed that this gentleman’s arguments, which came from nothing but the flesh, could have prevailed on him so far as to make him leave the right road. When he had finished, he turned to Evangelist again and spoke to this effect.

“Sir, what do you think? Is there any hope? May I go back now and go up to the Wicket Gate? Won’t I be abandoned for this, and sent away from there in disgrace? I’m sorry I listened to this man’s advice. But can my sin be forgiven?”

“Your sin is very great,” said Evangelist, “for by it you have committed two evils: you have abandoned the good road, and you have walked in forbidden paths. Yet the man at the gate will receive you, for he has good will toward men. Only,” he said, “be careful not to turn aside again, ‘or you will perish in the way, for his wrath can flare up in a moment.’” [Ps. 2:12]

Then Christian set himself to go back; and Evangelist kissed him, gave him one smile, and wished him Godspeed. So he went on in haste, and spoke to no one on the way; and if anyone asked him anything, he would not give them an answer. He walked like a man treading on forbidden ground the whole time, and could not feel safe at all until he was back on the road he had left to follow Mr. Worldly Wiseman’s advice. So in time Christian came up to the gate. Over the gate was written: Knock, and it shall be opened to you. [Matt. 7:8]
